units.translation: where the scholiast has καθαράν, κεχωρισμένην · ἢ αὐγάζοντα καὶ ὁρῶντα [pure, separated; or shining and seeing]. This second interpretation suits the adjective εὐαυγῆ [bright, gleaming], which Hemsterhuis restored by a sufficiently probable conjecture in Musgrave's note on Euripides Suppl. 652; Elmsley vainly attacked his opinion in his note on Euripides Bacch. 660, and L. Dindorf rightly defended it in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 2177.
For he held the seat of the whole army, bright and pure.
pure, separated; or shining and seeing
easy to carry in the arms
easy to carry in the arms
a burden not easy to carry in the arms.
You led a blessed life among the Persians, like a god.
having brave men, abounding in brave men
having brave men, abounding in brave men
with fortunes rich in brave men.
he held the mouth easily governed by the reins.
which (river) you must not cross; for it is not easy to cross.

Herodian in Arcadius p. 51, 21 attests the trisyllabic form Εὐβοικός [Euboean] (for Εὐβοϊκός [Euboean]), among words of more than two syllables ending in οικος [oikos], citing Εὐβοικός [Euboean]; another example is in Euripides Hel. 767 τὰ Ναυπλίου τ᾽ Εὐβοικὰ πυρπολήματα [the Euboean fire-signals of Nauplius], commonly written Εὐβοϊκά [Euboean].
For taking a Euboean sword, self-sharpened.
where Εὐβοιίδα [Euboean] at the beginning of a trimeter is contracted to Εὐβοῖδα [Euboean], as Εὐβοῖδα χώραν [Euboean land] is in Sophocles Trach. 74; on which see the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 2201.
metaphor taken from dice-players. Thus Porson for εὐβούλως [with good counsel].
And now Orestes, for he was fortunate in his throw, carrying his foot out of the destructive mud.
and never consider self-will better than prudence.
and best in soul and conspicuous for nobility.
in the absence of the noble lion.
gifted with a good tongue, i.e. eloquent
gifted with a good tongue, i.e. eloquent
in the bloom of youth with an eloquent mind.
and do not begrudge me my prayers.
trembling creeps over me as I hear the prayers.

where M in the first hand has εὐδαίμων [blessed], but with the letter o written above by a second hand. In several copies εὐδαῖμον [blessed] is found, contrary to the rule of Herodian in Choeroboscus on Theodosius p. 438, 30.
Lord Atreides, an old and blessed man.
He who is truly blessed should remain at home.
No one of the blessed hears these things.
You tell me things no less lamentable.
